summary.text: 东 means “east” and is the simplified form of 東, adapted from its cursive writing. Its present strokes are not separate 日 and 木 components. The proposed early history of 東 remains disputed.

formation.text: Derived: 东 is a cursive-derived form of 東. A major analysis interprets early 東 forms as a tied bag and proposes that this sign was reused to write the word for “east” because the bag’s name and the direction word sounded alike or similar. The bag interpretation is disputed, and the object’s ancient name and pronunciation are not established, so the proposed sound match remains unverified. A historically influential account instead explains 東 through 木 and 日 within 木; that interpretation does not prove how the early graph originated.

components.text: 东 is treated as a whole graph derived from cursive 東, not as a combination of independent 日 and 木 components.

history.text: 东 is adapted from cursive writing of 東. The oracle-style and Shang bronze-style images are modern redraws of early-form traditions; the seal-style image represents the later Shuowen tradition. They show different forms, but do not establish a step-by-step sequence.

Shuowen preserves the historical explanation that 東 is formed from 木 and was also understood as 日 within 木. This influential reading is not confirmation of the early graph’s origin; modern analyses reject it as a sufficient explanation, while a counteranalysis discusses possible 日 and 木 readings without establishing them as the origin.

uncertainties.text: The tied-bag interpretation is a significant but disputed account of early 東. Many early occurrences are reported in names and ritual contexts rather than in clear uses meaning “bag,” so the graph’s original referent remains unsettled.

The proposed reuse of a bag sign for “east” depends on a sound resemblance between the object’s name and the direction word. The object’s ancient name and pronunciation are not recovered here; reconstructions of 東 alone cannot establish them.

An oracle-bone use of 東 for the eastern region is reported, though the cited inscription was not independently inspected as an artifact. The received poem also uses 東 directionally, but its composition date and earliest physical witness are unresolved.

senses.period: Early inscriptional contexts reported; exact first attestation unresolved
senses.text: 東 is reported in an oracle-bone inscription for the eastern region, as well as in later early inscriptions referring to eastern territory. The received poem 小星 also uses it directionally, but its exact composition date and earliest physical witness are unresolved.

東 is also recorded with the meaning “host” or “landlord.” A traditional explanation links this sense to the host’s position on the east side, and a Tang literary example is reported. The first attestation and the path from “east” to this sense are unresolved.
The common modern meaning is the east or something situated toward the east.

limitations.text: The proposed bag-name origin is an account of reusing a written sign for a similar-sounding word, not a demonstrated semantic change; the source word’s name and sound remain unknown here.

The host or landlord explanation and its reported literary example do not establish a dated development from “east.” Spring and toilet senses also appear in dictionary records, but their chronology and semantic links are unresolved.

overview.text: 东 means “east” and comes from cursive writing of 東. One proposed account says 東 first pictured a tied bag, then was reused for “east” because the words sounded alike; the object’s name and the sound match remain uncertain.

components.text: Treat 东 as one graph derived from cursive 東; its strokes are not separate 日 and 木 parts.

relationships.text: 东 is adapted from cursive writing of 東; the precise dated path is unresolved.
